source.title: Theory III: Dynamics and Generalization in Deep Networks.
source.authors: Andrzej Banburski; Q. Liao; B. Miranda; Lorenzo Rosasco; Bob Liang; J. Hidary; T. Poggio

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. The appendix includes figure captions and flattened figure material, but that does not prevent reading the paper.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own CIFAR-10 training results relevant to whether deep networks fit training data, using cross-entropy and gradient descent rather than the version's SGD/Adam benchmark recipes. It also discusses theoretical dynamics under exponential loss, but does not test most version-specific conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper's own CIFAR-10 experiments are reported in figure captions and figure-associated text. Figure 2 says networks trained with different initializations, including randomized labels, have zero training classification error. Figures 10 and 11 describe training to 100% training accuracy on 100 CIFAR-10 datapoints, with and without batch normalization. Do not count related-work claims about other studies, theoretical assumptions, or values used only to describe experimental setup as additional results.
record.test_reason: The study's own convolutional-network experiments report zero CIFAR-10 training classification error, including randomized labels, bearing on V1 through a different gradient-training recipe. It does not test depth degradation, initialization-dependent training speed, or batch normalization's speed and learning-rate advantages.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors argue that, assuming training has already reached separability, continuous gradient flow under exponential-type loss implicitly controls normalized ReLU weights and approaches margin-maximizing stationary solutions. They connect this control to generalization, while acknowledging that pre-separability dynamics and finite-sample classification-error guarantees remain unresolved. Their empirical training-fit observations do not establish the separability assumption generally.
record.recipe_differences: The reported CIFAR-10 experiments use gradient descent on cross-entropy and a 100-example subset, rather than the claim versions' specified SGD/Adam benchmark comparisons. The paper's main theoretical analysis concerns continuous gradient flow on separable data under exponential-type loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch-normalization presence differs between the Figure 10 and Figure 11 training examples; both captions report 100% training accuracy. Figure 2 also distinguishes different weight initializations and randomized labels.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 16 and Figures 5–6 compare convergence of normalized weight directions under standard gradient descent and weight normalization in linear networks; the simplified analysis also equates batch and weight normalization in the one-layer case.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization can change convergence rates of weight directions toward margin solutions in separable linear classification.

fits_no_version.finding: Figures 2 and 9 examine initialization scale, normalized losses, and test performance without comparing training speed or trainable depth.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization scale and subsequent network normalization affect relationships between training loss and test performance.

record.problems: The CIFAR-10 training examples use a subset of 100 datapoints, not the full benchmark. Results are conveyed through figure captions and figures rather than a results table, and no uncertainty estimates or controlled comparison of training speed are reported. The Figure 10 and Figure 11 captions describe different experiments, so they do not establish a matched normalization comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results omitted. The paper discusses theoretical results and cites prior optimization claims, which are not the paper's own empirical results. Figures 3–9 concern dynamics, convergence rates, or test-loss relationships rather than training classification error for these versions.

untested.parts: CIFAR-100; controlled SGD/Adam comparisons; model-size thresholds; early stopping; and smaller or regularized recipes. R2 and R3 cover only 100 CIFAR-10 examples; Figure 2's sample size is unspecified.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious-minimum frequencies, and the effect of adding student neurons.
Depth-dependent training degradation, longer-training controls, identity-shortcut comparisons, very deep plain tanh training, and Fixup.
Activation-matched initialization effects on training speed or trainable depth, and orthogonal-versus-Gaussian training comparisons.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, loss recovery, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence.
Matched comparisons of accuracy gain or learning-rate tolerance with and without batch normalization, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the V3 and V6 limits_scope verdicts: successful fitting without normalization does not test depth degradation, and missing speed comparisons provide no evidence against batch normalization's acceleration claim. The study is not an original source for V1.

versions.untested_parts: Only CIFAR-10 results are reported; CIFAR-100, SGD or Adam specifically, model size thresholds, training duration comparisons, early stopping, and smaller or regularized recipes are not tested.
The paper does not compare plain and residual networks, vary depth, report ImageNet results, or test whether longer training changes a depth-related training error difference.
The CIFAR-10 caption reports training accuracy but not training speed or learning-rate tolerance; it does not test sigmoid MNIST, VGG CIFAR-10, Inception ImageNet, or Fixup.
